title: PVLEGS: A Public Speaking Acronym that Transforms Students
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. introduces PVLEGS, Erik Palmer's acronym for the performance side of speaking: Poise, Voice, Life, Eye contact, Gestures, and Speed. He argues that speaking and listening are neglected in K-12 schooling even though employers rank oral communication among the top skills they want, and that delivery matters as much as content because brilliant ideas are worthless if the speaker cannot deliver them. He walks through each element with Palmer's explanations and the mini-lessons he uses, stressing that poise and the other elements are learnable skills built through frequent required speaking. He then models the habit he wants from students by filming and critiquing his own keynote against PVLEGS, admitting flat delivery and too much reading from the page. The closing claim is that honest, even painful, self-analysis is the route to improvement, and teachers must model it by normalizing mistakes.
points: Speaking is a performance-based skill that K-12 schooling rarely teaches explicitly, so a simple shared vocabulary like PVLEGS makes it teachable and assessable.
Poise is framed as a skill rather than a trait, and the most basic way to build it is requiring students to speak often, which turns early fear into confidence by year's end.
PVLEGS covers delivery only, not speech content, so it pairs with separate instruction on organizing and expressing ideas.
Stuart models the method by critiquing his own filmed keynote, showing how teachers can make ruthless self-assessment normal for students.
quotes: Palmer begins his book with a simple question: examine a given week in your adult life, and tell me what percentage of your communication is written, and what percentage is spoken?
How a speech is performed may be more important than how it is built. If the speaker cannot deliver the speech well, no one will ever notice how well it was written.
The key breakthrough for my students here, initially, was that poise is a skill — it’s a thing you can learn, practice, and improve.
I have kids with intense fear of public speaking at the start of each year, and all of them are confident by the end. This isn’t magical Mr. Stuart; it’s giving them the gift of experience.
There are three elements of voice students work on: volume, enunciation, and avoiding odd vocal patterns like ending each sentence with a questioning tone or fading away at the end of each sentence

Exercises like the one I just engaged in — looking back at a filmed speaking performance and analyzing it closely for strengths and weaknesses — hurt. Few things are as painful as watching how you speak;
And yet, the only way we can become great at anything — at speaking, at teaching, at writing, at living — is by being ruthlessly honest about what we see in our performance.
